Part 2
Why the official numbers look calm
If the cuts are real, why is unemployment 4.1%? Because of what that number leaves out.
“But unemployment is only 4.1%”
True. It is also the number least able to see this. The headline rate counts people who looked for work in the last four weeks and found none. Walk down from it.
Headline unemployment (U-3).
Active job seekers only.
Add the underemployed (U-6).
Part-timers who want full-time work, and people who have stopped looking for now.
Recent college graduates in jobs that do not need the degree.
A graduate pouring coffee counts as fully employed.
Labor force participation.
It was 63.3% in February 2020. Someone who stops looking leaves the unemployment rate entirely. Part of this drop is an aging population. The next rung takes retirees out.
Men aged 25 to 54 who are neither working nor looking.
In the 1950s it was about 2%. These are not retirees or students.
The job that was never posted.

When a role is automated through attrition, nobody is laid off. Someone leaves and the opening is never listed. Headcount shrinks, the work is gone, and the unemployment rate does not move. It lands on the people who would have been hired: the third rung above.
“The easiest people to fire are the people you have not hired yet.”
, September 2026
The immigration factor.
A smaller labor pool also holds the unemployment rate down while hiring slows. Fewer people looking means a lower rate by definition.

We’ve been in a white-collar recession since the pandemic — with a brief reprieve in 2022. In 2025, if you strip out healthcare, the U.S. economy net lost jobs. That’s the definition of a recession, just not one any official body called. In 2026, we’re actively shedding jobs — and now it’s visible even in the headline numbers. The AI displacement didn’t start this. But it turned a slow leak into a flood.
The U.S. added 116,000 net new jobs in all of 2025 in current BLS data (
). Health care alone added 387,000, and 686,000 with social assistance.
Strip out healthcare, and the rest of the American economy net lost jobs.
So when someone says “AI will create new jobs” — we actually know what those jobs are. They’re nursing jobs.

Where is the breaking point?

Nobody knows. 100 would mean all six at their worst at the same moment, which has never happened. The index reached 71 in Nov 2009 and 80 in Apr 2020. Both times the job market recovered and the index fell. The wealth and wage measures are at their extremes anyway. For a sense of what breaking has looked like: in 1933, about 25% of American workers were unemployed (
). The summer before, the Army cleared jobless veterans out of Washington.

The Second Wave
We document what companies announce. Nobody tracks what happens next — and what happens next is larger.
THIS ALREADY HAPPENED. IN SLOW MOTION.

When manufacturing left Ohio and Michigan in the 1980s, it took 20 years for the full damage to show. The steel mill closed, then the diner across from it, then the school tax base, then the hospital wing. Economists called it job multiplier collapse. 4.7 million manufacturing jobs vanished — and dragged an estimated 7–8 million more with them.
AI displacement is the same mechanism. Compressed into years, not decades. And it’s not hitting Youngstown — it’s hitting San Francisco, New York, Seattle, Austin, and Boston simultaneously.

The barista problem:

The 547,016 jobs in this tracker are the ones whose companies issued press releases. For each of them, there are service workers — the lunch spots, dry cleaners, gyms, and Ubers near the office — whose customer base quietly vanished. Those jobs don’t get a press release. They get a lease non-renewal.
The geography trap:

Manufacturing displacement was regionally contained — you could point to Youngstown, Gary, Detroit. AI displacement is concentrated in the cities with the highest cost of living: SF, NYC, Seattle, Austin, Boston. The places that grew fastest on knowledge-worker salaries are now losing the income that made their housing math work. The real estate correction follows the labor correction. It already started.

Part 5
The best case against us
A page like this should be argued with. These are the strongest replies we know.
The best objections
Each of these is partly right. If we cannot answer them, you should not believe the rest of this page. Open any one to read our reply.
“AI automates tasks, not jobs. A job is a bundle of tasks.”
What is true
Almost no job can be handed over whole. People keep the parts that need judgment and trust.
What it misses
A team of 100 that loses 60% of its tasks does not keep 100 people on the remaining 40%. The job survives. Most of the jobs do not.
“Technology has always created more jobs than it destroyed.”
It has. About four in ten American workers farmed in 1900. Fewer than two in a hundred do now, and the country is richer for it.
That shift took generations, and it was not gentle while it happened. This one is measured in years, and it is the first to do the thinking work that people moved into last time.
“Cheaper means more demand. Look at radiologists.”
Where people want far more of something than they can afford, lower cost grows the field. Radiology is hiring.
It only works where demand is nowhere near full. Nobody files more insurance claims because claims got cheaper to process.
“The World Economic Forum expects 170 million new jobs against 92 million displaced.”
That is the forecast: worldwide, from every cause and not AI alone, by 2030.
A net figure hides who. The new jobs are not offered to the people displaced, in the place they live, at the pay they had. And an American salary is among the most expensive to keep.
“New business formation is booming. People are becoming founders.”
Applications are running at about 500,000 a month, well above 2019.

Businesses that hire are growing about half as fast: the Census Bureau expects 5.6% of applications to become employers within a year, down from 6.9% in 2019. A laid-off analyst who registers a consulting company counts as a new business.
“Companies are already rehiring. Look at Klarna.”
Klarna did walk it back. In May 2025 its chief executive said the cost focus had lowered quality, and the company began hiring people for customer service again.
A reversal belongs on the record next to the cut, and we log the ones we find. Rehiring some of a team is not rehiring the team.
“Half of these ‘AI layoffs’ are ordinary cost cuts with a better story.”
Some are. That is AI washing, and it is why only part of our count is marked confirmed.
It cuts the other way too: most displacement never becomes a layoff at all. That is why the stronger evidence on this page is about hiring, not firing.
What would change our mind
We would be glad to be wrong. If these turn, we will say so here.

How we count:

each layoff round is counted once. Where this number is too high:
Companies sometimes cite AI for cuts that are really about cost or over-hiring. Likely and unclear events are our judgment, not the company's statement.
Where it is too low:

Our tracker captures only public announcements. The majority of AI displacement happens invisibly — through attrition, contract non-renewals, and quiet eliminations never reported in the press. Our 547,016 tracks what was announced. Hiring that never happened is not in it.
